hops.title: Sand, blue dye and dead organizers that made salamander brains
hops.text: In the 1930s, labs racing to bottle the organizer's brain-making chemical got results that made no sense. Organizers killed by heat or alcohol still turned salamander ectoderm into nervous tissue. So did methylene blue dye. So did grains of sand. Then in the 1940s Lester Barth, and after him Johannes Holtfreter, found that pieces of spotted salamander ectoderm could form brain tissue in a simple saline culture, with no organizer at all. That set the field back for decades. In 2007 Cecilia Hurtado and Eddy De Robertis revisited it. Ectoderm attached to glass showed sustained MAPK activity, and blocking MAPK sharply reduced neural differentiation there; sand raised MAPK activity too.

sources.citation: De Robertis, E. M. (2009). Spemann's organizer and the self-regulation of embryonic fields. Mechanisms of Development 126(11-12):925-941 (PMC2803698).
Hurtado, C., & De Robertis, E. M. (2007). Neural induction in the absence of organizer in salamanders is mediated by MAPK. Developmental Biology 307(2):282-289.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A glass dish with a small square of pale embryonic tissue resting flat on the glass beside a bottle of blue dye and a pinch of sand on a wooden bench.
image.caption: Sand, blue dye and culturing on glass neuralized salamander ectoderm; glass-attached ectoderm showed sustained MAPK activity, and sand raised it.

hops.title: Noggin, big-headed tadpoles and fused finger joints
hops.text: William Smith and Richard Harland named noggin in 1992, slang for head. Its RNA rescued frog embryos that would otherwise have lacked a head, and at high doses gave them too much head. The same BMP catcher has a quieter job in human hands. In developing fingers, Noggin restrains BMP signaling so joints can form. With too little working Noggin, excess cartilage can develop at prospective joints, and bones can fuse at affected middle knuckles. Harvey Cushing described this inherited straight-finger trait in a large Virginia family in 1916. In 1999, geneticists found mutations in the human noggin gene in several families with it.

sources.citation: Smith, W. C., & Harland, R. M. (1992). Expression cloning of noggin, a new dorsalizing factor localized to the Spemann organizer in Xenopus embryos. Cell 70(5):829-840.
Gong, Y. et al. (1999). Heterozygous mutations in the gene encoding noggin affect human joint morphogenesis. Nature Genetics 21(3):302-304.
Plett, S. K. et al. (2008). Cushing proximal symphalangism and the NOG and GDF5 genes. Pediatric Radiology 38(2):209-215.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tadpole with an oversized head in a glass bowl beside a wooden mannequin hand with straight fingers.
image.caption: Extra Noggin can enlarge a frog embryo's head; in humans, Noggin restrains BMP signaling so finger joints can form.

hops.afterHeading: The same contest in a fly, upside down
hops.title: The vein in a shrimp is on the wrong side
hops.text: Next time you eat peeled shrimp, look at the dark thread cooks pull out along the curved back. It is called a vein, but it is the intestine, which in a shrimp runs along the dorsal side, the same side as its heart. The main nerve cord is on the opposite side: a paired cord running along the belly, between the muscle masses. So a shrimp carries its gut above its nerve cord, the reverse of you. Turn it over and the nerve cord sits above the gut, as in a vertebrate. In fly and frog embryos, the low-BMP side where neural tissue can form is flipped the same way.

sources.citation: Fox, R. Invertebrate Anatomy Online: Farfantepenaeus aztecus (Brown Shrimp). Lander University.
De Robertis, E. M., & Sasai, Y. (1996). A common plan for dorsoventral patterning in Bilateria. Nature 380(6569):37-40.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A peeled cooked shrimp lying on its side on a white plate beside a fork and a lemon wedge.
image.caption: In a shrimp's abdomen, the intestine lies above the nerve cord; in vertebrates, the spinal cord lies above the gut.
